summary: Wilde courted Florence Balcombe of Clontarf from August 1876, when he drew her and described taking 'an exquisitely pretty girl' of seventeen to afternoon cathedral service, through two Dublin years he later called 'the sweetest of all the years of my youth'. On learning of her engagement to Bram Stoker in autumn 1878 he asked back the gold cross he had given her one Christmas, returned her letters, and insisted on parting 'under your mother's roof'. In January 1881 he secretly sent her a crown of flowers via Ellen Terry for her Lyceum debut - 'She thinks I never loved her, thinks I forget. My God how could I!' - and in 1893 he sent her Salome 'with kind regards to Bram'. The editors caption her plate 'Wilde's first love'.

sources.quote: I need hardly say that I would not ask it from you if it was anything you valued, but worthless though the trinket be, to me it serves as a memory of two sweet years – the sweetest of all the years of my youth – and I should like to have it always with me. … whatever happens I at least cannot be indifferent to your welfare: the currents of our lives flowed too long beside one another for that. We stand apart now, but the little cross will serve to remind me of the bygone days, and though we shall never meet again, after I leave Ireland, still I shall always remember you at prayer. Adieu and God bless you.
sources.context: Wilde to Florence Balcombe, Monday night [? 30 September 1878], 1 Merrion Square North - asking back the gold cross he had given her 'one Christmas morning long ago', on learning of her engagement; the quoted run continues across the page-turn to the close of the letter
sources.supports: The participant's own naming of what the relationship was: two sweet years, 'the sweetest of all the years of my youth', and lives whose currents 'flowed too long beside one another' to leave him indifferent
sources.citation_provenance: PDF pp. 98-99. Elisions drop the arrangements for handing the cross back (via her sister Philippa) and the closing sentence about never meeting again.

sources.quote: I am just going out to bring an _exquisitely pretty girl_ to afternoon service in the Cathedral. She is just seventeen with the _most perfectly beautiful face I ever saw_ and not a sixpence of money. I will show you her photograph when I see you next.
sources.context: Wilde to Reginald Harding, Sunday [6 August 1876], 1 Merrion Square North; underlining in the original; the editors' note reads 'Almost certainly Florence Balcombe' - the identification is editorial
sources.supports: The courtship's opening, August 1876 (identification of the girl as Balcombe is the editors', marked 'almost certainly')

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote: The other – don't think me treacherous, Nellie – but the other please give to Florrie _from yourself_. I should like to think that she was wearing something of mine the first night she comes on the stage, that anything of mine should touch her. … She thinks I never loved her, thinks I forget. My God how could I!
sources.context: Wilde to Ellen Terry, [3 January 1881], Tite Street, Chelsea - sending two flower crowns, one to be given secretly to Florence, appearing that night in The Cup at the Lyceum; underlining in the original
sources.supports: Wilde's retrospective avowal of having loved her, two years after the parting
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 132. Elision drops two short sentences ('Of course if you think - but you won't think she will suspect? How could she?').

manuscript.repository: British Library, London (Lady Eccles Oscar Wilde Collection)

sources.quote: My dear Florence, Will you accept a copy of *Salomé* – my strange venture in a tongue that is not my own, but that I love as one loves an instrument of music on which one has not played before. You will get it, I hope, tomorrow, and I hope you will like it. With kind regards to Bram, believe me, always your sincere friend
sources.context: Wilde to Florence Balcombe Stoker, [Postmark 22 February 1893], Babbacombe Cliff; signed Oscar Wilde; Salomé italicized in original
sources.supports: Cordial contact persisting to 1893, fifteen years after the parting

manuscript.repository: University of Virginia Library, Charlottesville, Virginia

sources.quote:
My dear Florrie, I send you a line to wish you a pleasant Easter. A year ago I was in Athens and you sent me I remember a little Easter card - over so many miles of land and sea - to show me you had not forgotten me.

I have been greatly disappointed in not being able to come over, but I could only spare four days and as I was not feeling well came down here to try and get some ozone. The weather is delightful and if I had not a good memory of the past I would be very happy. I have a delightful friend (a *new* friend) with me and have written *one* sonnet, so am not so misanthropic as usual. I hope you are all well especially Gracie: Willie's success in the North is most encouraging. I send you an account of Bournemouth. Ever yours

OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Florence Balcombe, [April 1878], Royal Bath Hotel, Bournemouth (MS Clark). The editors note Easter Sunday 1878 fell on 21 April. The letter breaks where the printed page does and continues on the next folio. He is counting back a year to a card she sent him in Athens, which is the whole point of the letter: not the Easter wish but the remembering.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The courtship at its steadiest - a year measured by a card she sent.
